title: US and Canada Work on Deal to Ease Steel and Auto Tariffs
excerpt: Negotiators led by Howard Lutnick and Dominic LeBlanc are discussing relief from Section 232 duties of up to 50 percent on steel and 25 percent on autos, sources tell Reuters, possibly before November 3.
body:
• The United States and Canada are working on a deal to ease U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, six sources told Reuters, after trade talks collapsed in August.
  • The talks centre on Section 232 tariffs — up to 50 percent on Canadian steel and 25 percent on autos — led by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Canada’s Dominic LeBlanc.
  • One Canadian source said a steel and auto deal was possible before the November 3 U.S. midterm elections; U.S. sources said Washington wants further concessions from Canada.
  • Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney described only a “slight intensification” in talks and said Canada’s position has not changed.

The United States and Canada are working on a deal to ease U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, two U.S. and four Canadian sources told Reuters, as both governments try to repair relations after trade talks broke down in August. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because the negotiations are private.

The discussions are narrow by design. They focus on tariffs imposed under Section 232 of U.S. trade law, including up to 50 percent on Canadian steel and 25 percent on autos, with negotiators discussing potential relief from those duties. A broader trade pact is not what sources described — one Canadian industry source told Reuters a deal, if it comes, would likely be a narrowed one, and could come quickly.

Who is negotiating, and why Commerce leads

Because Section 232 tariffs are administered by the Commerce Department, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, rather than the U.S. Trade Representative’s office, sits at the centre of the talks, sources on both sides of the border said. Lutnick and Dominic LeBlanc, Canada’s minister responsible for Canada-U.S. trade, have been in regular contact recently, one source said. The USTR’s office and Canada have also been in contact in recent days on the overall architecture of any deal, a USTR official said.

https://x.com/LarkDavis/status/2114880048956072093

LeBlanc’s office did not confirm details. “Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities,” a spokesperson said. “We stand ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada’s interests.” The White House and Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Carney plays down an imminent deal

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney offered a cooler public read on Monday. He said there had been “a slight intensification” in talks with the United States, that Ottawa had not changed its stance, and, in Reuters’ account, that any progress reflected the U.S. coming closer to Canada’s position. Reporting by Dow Jones via Morningstar added that Carney said a deal is possible so long as the U.S. moves toward Canada’s demands, and that any pact must include relief on steel, aluminum and automobiles.

That gap — “very close” signals from Washington and caution from Ottawa — is the central uncertainty. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett had said negotiations were gathering steam, and President Donald Trump predicted at a rally on Sunday that the dispute would be resolved “soon,” without specifics, Reuters reported.

Politics and the November 3 deadline

The timing is political on the U.S. side. Reuters reported Trump faces low approval — 32 percent in the polling it cited — and his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, with Republican candidates in border states calling for an end to the trade war with Canada. One Canadian source said a steel and auto deal was possible before November 3; U.S. sources said the administration wanted Canada to make further concessions.

The stakes rise if talks fail. Talks collapsed in August over issues including duties on medium- and heavy-duty vehicles critical for Canadian factories, and U.S. automakers had hoped for relief from the 25 percent tariffs raising the cost of shipping vehicles and parts across the border. Trump has previously said he would raise tariffs on steel and auto imports from Canada to 50 percent from January 1, 2027, and on Friday he signed an order removing 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products, a move Reuters said could benefit businesses in Maine.

What happens next

Watch for any announcement before November 3, and for whether relief covers aluminum as well as steel and autos, as Carney has demanded. For cross-border workers and businesses in Ontario’s steel and auto corridor — including the many South Asian Canadians employed in manufacturing, logistics and parts supply around the Greater Toronto Area and Windsor — even a narrowed Section 232 deal would lower costs that are now built into vehicles and parts moving across the border each day. Until a text is announced, the tariffs in place remain 50 percent on steel and 25 percent on autos.
